#5077. Crosschain protocol Across restores systems after domain hijack

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Security platform GoPlus reported that total user losses are estimated at $350,000, with funds stolen from wallets on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, BNB Chain, Ink, and Plasma.

Crosschain interoperability protocol Across Across Protocol (ACX) has restored control of its website and resumed normal operations on Wednesday after a domain takeover that redirected visitors to a phishing site.

At around 18:45 UTC on Nov. 10, attackers gained control of the protocol's official domain through a social engineering attack on its domain registrar, Namecheap, Across said in a post on X.

Across said it received an alert within 15 minutes of the takeover and began efforts to take the site offline. Security response group SEAL911 flagged it as a phishing domain with major wallet providers, while Cloudflare marked the domain at risk and subsequently removed its DNS records, rendering the phishing site inaccessible.

While Across did not disclose the number of impacted users or losses, security platform GoPlus reported that total user losses are estimated at $350,000, with funds stolen from wallets on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, BNB Chain, Ink, and Plasma.

GoPlus detailed that the phishing page lured users into signing fake token approvals or permits designed to drain wallets.

Later on Wednesday, Across announced that it had regained control of the domain with assistance from Namecheap, and restored all systems to normal operations. It added that all affected users would be made whole.

Separately, decentralized exchange Arcus said on Tuesday that it lost around $2.23 million in USDG stablecoins due to an accounting bug that allowed an account to record a larger balance than it actually held. The exploiter requested another $3 million in withdrawals that were prevented by the rate limit on its bridge.

The DEX said no other user accounts were impacted, and it has fully covered the temporary shortfall with the company treasury.

Suiball, a Sui-native hardware wallet project, also announced closure on Tuesday, after the Sui Foundation decided that backing the project was too risky due to a recent wave of attacks on crypto hardware wallets.

These incidents follow a surge in security breaches and phishing campaigns accelerated by AI tools that enable faster and more sophisticated attacks. DefiLlama data shows $8.78 billion has been lost across 341 crypto hacks and exploits year-to-date, led by a $6.36 billion breach at Binance.

#5074. Goldman, Citi and Global Banks Commit $270 Million to Challenge Crypto’s Stablecoin Giants

Goldman, Citi and Global Banks Commit $270 Million to Challenge Crypto’s Stablecoin Giants

The group of global banks building a joint stablecoin has put real money on the table, committing around $270 million to fund the venture as it moves from blueprint to buildout.

Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Banco Santander, and Deutsche Bank are among the institutions backing the effort, Bloomberg reported Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The capital is meant to cover five years of operations for a planned U.S.-incorporated company that will issue a dollar-denominated stablecoin. Known among participants as Project Faro, the venture is still searching for a chief executive, and its final name remains under discussion.

A spokesperson for the project declined to comment, as did Santander and Deutsche Bank, while Goldman and Citi referred questions to the project.

The funding is the concrete next step for an initiative that first went public late last year. As Decrypt previously reported, 21 of the world’s largest financial institutions committed in September to form a company to issue a U.S. dollar stablecoin, targeting a launch in the first half of 2027, with a euro version and other currencies to follow.

That consortium had more than doubled from an initial group of 10 banks that began exploring the idea in October 2025, and now spans North America, Europe, East Asia, the Middle East and Africa.

Beyond the four named by Bloomberg, its participants include Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Fidelity Investments, PNC, Capital One, TD Bank, UBS, BBVA, Deutsche Bank, Lloyds Banking Group and MUFG, among others. JPMorgan, notably, is not on the list.

The venture is one of several collaborative pushes by established finance into a business long dominated by crypto-native players. Visa, Mastercard and Stripe are among more than 100 companies backing the issuer Open Standard, while European banks have formed Qivalis to issue a euro-denominated coin.

At the moment, Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC together account for about 85% of a market worth roughly $290 billion, nearly all of it dollar-pegged. When the bank consortium first went public in September, Circle’s stock fell about 6% as investors priced in the prospect of bank-backed competition for USDC.

The banks are betting that institutional trust, regulatory alignment and existing client networks can win them a share of a settlement business that promises round-the-clock, cross-border payments at lower cost than traditional rails.

The token is being designed to comply with the U.S. GENIUS Act, which created the first federal framework for dollar-pegged tokens in 2025, and, where applicable, the EU’s MiCA regime. The group has said it wants the stablecoin used across wholesale, institutional and retail markets.

For now, Project Faro remains pre-launch, with no issued token, no named CEO, not even a final name, and a 2027 target that leaves ample room for delay.

But the $270 million commitment marks a shift, and a concrete signal that this bank consortium intends to compete for the onchain dollar rather than leave it to crypto.

#5073. Crypto ally Tom Emmer elected House GOP minority whip

The Minnesota lawmaker, who helped establish the Congressional Crypto Caucus, will stay on as Republican whip after Democrats won the midterms.

Pro-crypto US Representative Tom Emmer has been elected House Republican minority whip, securing the party’s second-highest leadership position as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January.

Emmer beat Texas Representative August Pfluger in a 103-76 secret ballot vote, according to Politico. He previously served as House Republican majority whip and will remain the party’s No. 2 leader, this time under incoming Minority Leader Jim Jordan.

As minority whip, Emmer will be responsible for rallying Republican votes, coordinating the party’s legislative strategy and helping maintain unity on key bills.

Emmer has been a leading Republican voice on digital assets. In March 2025, he and Representative Ritchie Torres announced the bipartisan Congressional Crypto Caucus, aimed at mobilizing support for digital asset legislation, including stablecoin and market structure bills.

He is also an original cosponsor of the CLARITY Act and introduced the Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act, which seeks to clarify that blockchain developers and infrastructure providers who do not control customer funds are not money transmitters under federal law.

“Tom has been one of the strongest advocates for digital assets in Congress, and he has led the fight against a government-controlled CBDC and stood up for American innovators,” GOP Senator Cynthia Lummis said on X.

#5072. Bitcoin and Blockchain Basics

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

How the First Cryptocurrency Works in Practice

Bitcoin is a decentralized digital currency that operates on a peer-to-peer network and is secured through Proof of Work. Its blockchain is a public ledger made up of blocks of transactions, with each block referencing the previous block’s hash to create a verifiable, tamper-evident history. Private keys allow users to authorize the spending of their Bitcoin. Wallet software manages these keys, constructs and signs transactions, and broadcasts them to the network, where nodes independently verify them.

Bitcoin and blockchain basics are the starting point for understanding the cryptocurrency industry. This Campus 101 subject explores where Bitcoin came from, how a blockchain records transactions, why decentralization matters, how mining secures the network, and how users control and send Bitcoin.

The lesson summaries below give a short overview of the full course content. Take the full interactive Bitcoin & Blockchain Basics 101 course to explore each lesson in more depth through guided explanations, examples, and activities.

Establishes Bitcoin and blockchain as the starting point for understanding mining, monetary policy, wallets, transactions, and the wider crypto industry.

Connects Bitcoin’s creation to the 2008 financial crisis, Satoshi Nakamoto’s whitepaper, decentralized money, and early contributors.

Defines Bitcoin as peer-to-peer digital money with a fixed supply, Proof of Work security, and transparent but pseudonymous transactions.

Uses a digital-notebook analogy to explain blocks, hashes, hash pointers, Merkle trees, tamper evidence, and verifiable ledgers.

Explains how miners perform Proof of Work, find valid hashes, add blocks, and earn block rewards and transaction fees.

Covers the 21 million supply cap, predictable issuance, block rewards, halvings, and Bitcoin’s scarcity model.

Introduces market capitalization, hash rate, and mining difficulty as different measures of market size and network activity.

Distinguishes backward-compatible soft forks from incompatible hard forks, using SegWit and Bitcoin Cash as examples.

Lesson 8 - Securing Communication and Information

Explains how private keys, public keys, and digital signatures establish control and authorize transactions.

Compares hardware and software wallets and explains addresses, private-key protection, and seed-phrase recovery.

Introduces UTXOs, inputs, outputs, change, fees, mempools, and the path from signing to confirmation.

Considers Bitcoin as peer-to-peer money, a store-of-value asset, a commodity-like asset, and the foundation of a wider decentralized economy.

Bitcoin launched during a turbulent economic period, when many people were losing trust in traditional financial markets. Cryptocurrency offered an alternative approach: a financial system designed to operate without central authorities, banks, or intermediaries.

Satoshi Nakamoto’s 2008 whitepaper, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, outlined the idea of a decentralized, trustless, censorship-resistant form of money. Satoshi’s identity remains unknown, but the network launched in 2009 and became the starting point for the broader cryptocurrency ecosystem.

Other important topics include early contributors and thought leaders, including educators, cryptographers, and early adopters who helped make Bitcoin understandable, secure, and culturally important.

Bitcoin is presented as the first cryptocurrency. It is a decentralized digital currency with a fixed supply of 21 million coins, a peer-to-peer network, Proof of Work security, and transparent but pseudonymous transactions.

The important beginner idea is not only that Bitcoin is digital money. It is that Bitcoin showed how a network could record value transfers without relying on a single company, government, or bank to update the ledger.

Decentralization means the distribution of power and control across a network, rather than relying on a single entity. In Bitcoin, thousands of independently operated nodes verify and store transaction data. This helps ensure that no single party can easily alter, censor, or control the network.

Instead of trusting one central database, the network relies on many participants to maintain and check the ledger.

A useful mental model is this: imagine a blockchain as a digital notebook. Each page of the notebook is a block. Each block contains information such as transaction data. Each block is assigned a unique code, called a hash, that identifies its contents.

Each block also points back to the previous block. That link is what creates the chain. If someone tries to change the contents of an already verified block, the hash changes, making tampering apparent to the rest of the network.

Within each block, Merkle trees combine transaction hashes into a compact commitment to the block’s contents. Rewriting confirmed history would require an attacker to redo the Proof of Work for the altered block and catch up with the honest network, which makes tampering increasingly difficult as more blocks are added.

Mining is introduced as the work that secures the ledger. In Proof of Work, network participants compete to solve computational puzzles. The first miner to find a valid solution earns the right to add a new block of transactions to the blockchain and receive compensation through newly issued Bitcoin and transaction fees.

Miners act as accountants competing to validate Bitcoin transactions. Mining rigs perform many calculations to find a nonce that creates a hash matching the difficulty set by the network. Other nodes then check whether the proposed block follows the rules before accepting it.

Bitcoin’s supply is capped at 21 million coins. New Bitcoin enters the network through mining rewards, and those rewards are reduced through events known as halvings. This creates a predictable supply schedule because no centralized party can simply change the issuance schedule on its own.

Several common metrics describe different parts of the system. Market capitalization combines price and circulating supply to estimate the market value of issued Bitcoin. Hash rate estimates the computational power contributing to mining, while mining difficulty adjusts the challenge of finding a valid block so issuance remains relatively consistent as hash rate changes.

The focus then moves from the network to the user. Bitcoin uses asymmetric cryptography, including private keys, public keys, and digital signatures, to prove ownership and authorize transactions without revealing the private key itself.

A private key is like a secret PIN, password, or physical key. Whoever controls the private key controls the wallet’s assets. A public key is derived from the private key and acts more like the lock or mailbox: it can be shared, but it does not reveal the private key.

A Bitcoin address is a public identifier derived from the public key. It is shorter and easier to share, and it is where someone can receive Bitcoin.

Software wallets run on connected devices and prioritize convenience, while hardware wallets keep signing keys in a dedicated device and reduce some forms of online exposure. Many wallets use a seed phrase as a recovery backup. Anyone who obtains the private key or seed phrase may be able to control the funds, so neither should be shared.

Bitcoin uses the UTXO model, which stands for Unspent Transaction Output. A paper-bill analogy makes it easier to understand: you must spend the whole output and receive change back if needed.

If Alice has one UTXO worth 2 BTC and wants to send 1 BTC to Bob, she spends the full 2 BTC output as the transaction input. The transaction creates one output to Bob and another output back to Alice as change. The original output is then marked as spent and cannot be used again.

Transaction fees help miners decide which transactions to include in blocks. If the network is busy and a fee is too low, the transaction may remain in the mempool, a temporary holding area for valid transactions that have not yet been included in a block.

Other important topics include the difference between soft forks and hard forks. A soft fork is a backward-compatible upgrade, meaning updated nodes can still interact with older nodes. A hard fork is not backward-compatible and can lead to separate chains if participants do not agree on the same rules.

The final point is that Bitcoin now plays several roles in the financial and technological landscape. It is often discussed as a store-of-value asset, a highly liquid digital asset, and the foundation that introduced a broader decentralized economy.

Bitcoin: The first cryptocurrency and a peer-to-peer digital monetary network.

Blockchain: A ledger made of linked blocks that record transaction data.

Node: A network participant that stores, checks, or relays Bitcoin data.

Proof of Work: A consensus mechanism where miners expend computational resources to add valid blocks.

Miner: A participant that competes to create new blocks and earn rewards and fees.

Hash: A unique code generated from data; changing the data changes the hash.

Private key: The secret credential that authorizes control of funds.

Public key: A public value derived from a private key and used in transaction verification.

Bitcoin address: A shareable identifier used to receive Bitcoin.

UTXO: An unspent transaction output that can be used as an input in a future transaction.

Mempool: A temporary area for valid transactions waiting to be included in a block.

#5068. 7 Best Work Totes, Tested by Style Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Finding the right work tote is surprisingly tough. It needs to be durable, secure, organized, comfortable, and, hopefully, stylish too. If you’re like our editors, you might be stuffing everything from water bottles to emergency umbrellas in your everyday bag. A good work tote may even be able to double as a carry-on or weekender bag.

While I work remotely, I’m often toting my work setup with me to my favorite coffee shop, coworking space, or a friend’s house to get work done. So, I know a thing or two about what matters when you’re looking for a durable bag that can securely hold all your everyday essentials (and more) for years without signs of wear and tear.

Work totes are some of the most functional bags you can own, too. The best work totes often reduce strain on your back and shoulders, since their handles make them easy to carry. They can also allow you to access the items you need most quickly. For example, most bags are designed with smaller pockets so you can easily store and grab your phone or wallet in a jiffy.

Not all work totes are created equal, though. A lack of functional pockets can make you feel disorganized, and straps that dig into your shoulders can make your commute miserable. Our Women’s Health editors tested more than 20 work totes and spoke to fashion experts to the find the best options for every budget.

From work to travel, the Apryl Laptop Tote Bag is the best overall work tote for its smart compartment placement, durability, and comfy straps. Even better: At $50, it’s budget-friendly, too. When our tester first ordered this bag, they didn’t have high expectations for it because of the affordable price point, but it quickly became the best tote they tested.

Our tester is obsessed with the bag’s comfort, which makes it easy to hold and tote. Made of faux leather, the bag has structured but flexible straps that don’t dig into your shoulders or hands, no matter how long you hold the bag. Inside the bag, you’ll find a padded laptop pocket that closes with Velcro to keep your device secure. There are also five additional smaller compartments inside (all cotton-lined), including a water bottle holder that’s also padded.

One thing I particularly love about this bag is that it’s also designed with two exterior compartments, one on each side of the bag, that each close with magnetic buttons. "I found these useful for throwing keys, and other items I don’t necessarily need throughout the day, like an emergency Tylenol," our tester says.

When you put the bag down, it lies flat, which makes it really easy to reach inside and find specific items. However, the bag doesn’t have studs at the bottom, so it does touch whatever you place it on. While the red color our tester received can hide stains or dirt fairly well, another color option, like the beige choice, may not.

I tested Quince’s Leather Shopper Tote, and it has quickly become my go-to work bag. While most bags on this list have a laptop pocket, this work tote has the best one. Its laptop compartment is lined in soft suede, which protects your device against scratches. I also like to throw my sunglasses in there, since I’m pretty bad about carrying their case, but I’m always afraid the keys in my bag will rough them up. What I love about this zippered laptop holder, which sits in the center of the purse, is that it also serves as the bag’s divider, essentially dividing the bag into two separate compartments. It’s almost like you have two purses.

I like using one side to store my work essentials, like my planner or other important documents, and the other for extras, like my makeup, hand cream, and, on rarer occasions, even a pair of shoes. Each side also has smaller compartments to increase your organization options: One side has two smaller compartments, while the other has just one. I do wish at least one of these compartments was zippered to keep small items, like my wallet, more secure during crowded commutes, but I just throw it in the same pocket as my laptop, and that works for me.

I also like that this bag is structured and more on the rigid side because it gives the bag a just-purchased feel, while giving me a more put-together look. I find that the straps are a little too thin, though, which, as a chronic overpacker, makes me worry about how much of a load the bag can really handle. I’ve had experiences where I’ve hung bags with thin straps onto hooks (like those inside a bathroom stall) only to have a strap detach from the bag, and it’s not the best experience. So while I do use some work totes for short weekend trips, this is one I would likely leave behind.

Still, it’s the perfect bag for professional settings or errand-running on weekends. Its price point of $150 is also exceptional for a bag made from real leather. Other options, like the Cuyana bag in this guide, are much more pricey.

Read More: Quince Italian Leather Tote Review

Amazon has a boatload of bags that look pricier than they are, and, at around $35, this work tote is just that. It’s designed with a crocodile pattern that gives the bag a stylish touch and high-end feel, which is what originally drew me to it, but it’s also one of the best-rated tote bags on the site. Like our best overall bag, it’s made with a padded laptop pocket that closes with a small Velcro strap, but there’s also a zipper compartment in the middle that’s big enough to store a laptop.

Inside the bag, you’ll find two small mesh pockets on the narrower sides, perfect for storing small valuables, pens, or travel makeup essentials. “On days I wore a watch to the office, I would take it off and store it in one of those pockets until it was time to leave (I find it hard to type and wear a link-chain watch at the same time because of the friction between my hand and the desk),” one tester says. “I also used those pockets to store cough drops, lip gloss, and other trinkets I didn’t want to get lost in the abyss of my work tote.”

There’s a smaller zippered pocket inside of the purse, which I appreciate for storing items you want to keep secure, like cash, plus two other smaller compartments for a phone, wallet, or other mid-sized items. For perspective, you could probably fit a bottle of perfume in each of them.

I also appreciate this bag’s versatility. It’s designed like an accordion, meaning it widens when stuffed to the brim, but appears narrower when it’s not packing a heavy load. The purse also comes with an additional strap, so you can detach the tote’s carrying handles and use it as a crossbody bag if that’s your preference.

Our tester’s only concern with this bag is that the gold accents on the straps may fade over time, which may make the bag unsightly. However, they have used it for over a month, including on rainy days, and have had no issues yet.

There’s just something about real leather that feels so luxe. That’s one of the reasons this leather tote from Cuyana is worth the splurge. The material feels soft and has proven to be durable, despite how much our tester stuffed this bag or threw it on the ground after a long day.

The bag features only one big compartment, which may be a con for some. (There is a smaller pocket inside—about twice the size of an iPhone plus—but nothing else besides that.) If you prefer a little more organization, you can buy accessories that attach to the inside of the bag using button clasps. These include zippered pockets of different sizes and a laptop compartment. “Though I don’t love having to pay more for these accessories, I do like that these make the bag’s design totally customizable,” our tester says.

Our tester used the bag without organizational pockets and was impressed at how much it could hold. “I’ve thrown a laptop, a pair of shoes, extra clothes, and my toiletry bag in there easily,” they say. “While I wouldn’t call this bag stretchy, its material is less structured, offering a little more give than other bags on this list.”

They particularly liked that the straps are built into the bag, instead of sewn onto it. “This gives me extra reassurance that this purse won’t fall apart on me when I’m on the go,” they say. “The straps are also pretty wide and flexible, so they feel very comfy on my shoulders, no matter how heavy the bag is.” It is a little tougher to wear this tote on your shoulder when wearing a thick, puffy coat, but it just takes a little more effort to throw on than some of the other bags on this list.

The Longchamp Le Pliage Tote is a cult-classic bag that you’ve probably noticed someone else carrying on your commute before. The large nylon tote with leather trim comes from a luxury French brand, which explains the higher price tag.

While it doesn’t offer a lot of internal organization—just two pockets—the large internal compartment is great for those who need to stash bulkier items, like an extra pair of shoes.

Plus, the water-resistant nylon exterior is flexible and durable, so you don’t have to worry about the elements as much as with an all-leather bag.

With the Le Pliage Tote, you’re paying for the Longchamp name and classic design, but you could definitely do worse than a bag as durable and functional as this one.

From one of our favorite luggage brands, the Monos Metro Tote is perfect for someone who travels frequently for work or fun. The vegan leather design is simple, yet stylish, and it comes in six colors to coordinate with your luggage set.

While it’s priced at nearly $250, the bag boasts the most extensive organization I’ve seen in a work tote, including a laptop compartment, water bottle holder, and handy exterior pocket for quickly stashing items during airport security. And the zipper closure to keep your belongings secure, whether commuting or jet-setting.

You may know Baggu for its reusable grocery totes, but the brand also makes durable purses and work totes in its signature slouchy, patterned nylon style. This shoulder bag is for someone who packs light and just needs a versatile, casual bag to carry a laptop and a few extra items.

The Baggu Shoulder Bag is a workhorse with a thick, adjustable strap, zipper closure, and a spot to attach your keys. The tote is completely machine washable, which is an anomaly among work bags. However, the bag’s main compartment is narrow with space for a 14-inch laptop and a slim notebook or two.

At around $50, it’s a great everyday bag and comes in a fun variety of colors and patterns, including leopard and gingham, for someone who wants to show a little personality at work.

While work bags are functional, we also want them to be stylish and versatile, so you don’t have to switch bags for a different outfit. Most of our favorite work totes are simple, timeless silhouettes with a few exceptions, like the Baggu Shoulder Bag for a slouchy look.

The material of your bag will often come down to style preference, but some materials are more functional than others. For example, canvas bags are durable, lightweight, and great for everyday use. That said, they do take a little more effort to clean when soiled, since canvas doesn’t dry quickly. You may need to give it some time to air out after spot cleaning.

Another option: Leather totes—these are chic and long-lasting. Just keep in mind that they can be pricier than other totes because they’re investment pieces that should last for years. They’re also versatile and stylish enough to take to post-work activities. (Read: You won’t look weird showing up to happy hour with this as your plus-one.)

Vegan leather is also a great option because it’s a more affordable and cruelty-free option, and some of them look pretty realistic. Just keep in mind that vegan leathers can be made from a variety of materials, and some are more durable than others. For example, some vegan leathers made from low-quality plastic are prone to peeling.

Finally, nylon or polyester bags are perfect for a more casual, sporty vibe. They are easy to clean and can really take a roughing up with day-to-day use.

Look for a bag with both larger and smaller compartments, which will make organizing and protecting your important items so much easier, says fashion contributor Rose Lauture. For example, the zippered laptop compartment in Quince’s Italian leather tote is lined with suede to avoid scratching it. Meanwhile, smaller compartments will prevent you from being forced to dig through all the random stuff that accumulates in a work tote to find your phone, pen, or lip gloss.

Think about how you use your tote bag when searching for the right size and organizational capabilities. For example, if you like to pack lunch or bring your gym clothes along, then you’ll need a bag with a wide open compartment for bulkier items. If your main goal is to stay organized and pack light, then a smaller bag with interior pockets may help you on the go.

The closure of the bag will depend on your needs. Totes with a zip or snap closure are great for securing your items and protecting them against thieves, Lauture says. It also ensures that your belongings won’t be scattered across the floor if the bag falls over. But if you prefer accessibility instead of security, open totes may be a more convenient option, she adds.

Having a work tote with comfortable straps can make or break your commute, whether you catch a train into the city or walk to and from your car. Look for bags with thick, durable straps that are tall enough so the bag doesn’t rub against your armpit. Some work totes even come with a crossbody option or adjustable strap, if you prefer to tailor the bag to your height.

I’m always working on the go, so I have a lot of experience carrying around work totes, from faux leather to canvas options. I did extensive research on work totes from top brands to come up with an initial list for this guide, choosing a variety of sizes, materials, and price points. I got hands-on with the runner-up tote from Quince, and one Women’s Health tester with more than 12 years of experience using work totes spent a month testing the other bags.

From commuting to weekend trips, I evaluated the work totes on factors like design, material, compartments, comfort, and more.

The cross-chain bridge said a social engineering attack targeting domain registrar Namecheap allowed hackers to redirect users to a phishing site.

Cross-chain bridge Across Protocol said it has regained control of its website after a social engineering attack on Tuesday enabled attackers to gain control of its domain, replacing its website with a phishing site.

In a post on Wednesday, Across said the across.to domain is back under their control with help from Namecheap founder Richard Kirkendall, and that all systems are now working normally.

“All affected users will be made whole. We’ll share a full post-mortem in the coming days,” the team said on X.

The update follows Across’s Tuesday warning to users to avoid its app amid reports of drained wallets. The total losses and number of affected users have not yet been disclosed.

In an earlier update, Across said a social engineering attack on its domain registrar, Namecheap, gave an attacker control of its domain at approximately 18:45 UTC.

The team said it was alerted within 15 minutes and immediately worked to shut the website down. Security response group SEAL911 helped flag the domain as phishing with major wallets, while Cloudflare marked it as at risk and later removed its DNS records.

Some users who visited the domain before the malicious site was fully blocked may have been affected, the team said. Third-party integrations and API users were unaffected.

The incident affected one of the largest cross-chain bridges by trading activity. Across ranked third by 30-day transfer volume, behind Circle and LayerZero, according to DefiLlama, having processed about $5.9 billion over the period.

#5062. I Spent Years Hiding My Ulcerative Colitis. One Night at Sundance Changed How I Saw My Disease

In an exclusive excerpt from her new book, NBC correspondent Chloe Melas shares the reality of navigating an early relationship with IBD.

For 15 years, I've battled a form of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) known as Ulcerative Colitis. It's an autoimmune disease in which your body attacks your colon. When I was diagnosed at 25-years-old after finding blood in my stool, I felt like I had nowhere to turn because neither side of my family has gut issues. I thought if maybe I ignored my symptoms (the blood, the bloating, the constipation), it would eventually go away. It didn't. As I continued to chase my career and search for love, things got worse and I eventually couldn't hide it anymore. When I went to the Sundance Film Festival I was at the height of my disease and I felt like it was following me like a cloud trying to rain on every moment of joy. What follows is a story—from my new book that I co-authored with Judy Batalion, The Girl’s Guide to Guts—that I never planned to share publicly. But I am now in hopes of helping anyone out there feel less alone. — Chloe Melas

As I rose up through the TV ranks, my invitations became better and better. I wasn’t at the end of the red carpets anymore; I was now just a few spots from the end! One of the best parts of the job is being able to attend some of the most exclusive events, like the Golden Globe Awards, private concerts, and the annual Sundance Film Festival, which, until 2026, was held at the foot of the Rocky Mountains in Park City, Utah. Sundance, started by the late actor Robert Redford, is a week-long party celebrating the best in film from that year, with a who’s who of Hollywood descending on this snowy, storybook town.

In 2012, worlds collided when (my now-husband) Brian and I first started dating, because he coincidentally hosted the hardest-to-get-into party at Sundance. Just a few months into dating, he invited me to come along. I said yes before even checking to see if I had enough vacation days. Somehow I convinced my editor that I should go and cover all the celebrity happenings. I also told her it would cost the company nothing because I had been invited by a film studio, which was a total lie—I put it all on my credit card and told myself I’d figure it out later. Luckily, she said yes!

Brian and I had already been on a few trips, but it was getting harder to pretend I was headed to the gym for a workout when I really was going to find a lobby loo. Eventually I had to come clean, because saying I was going to hit the gym at 11 p.m. after a couple of cocktails wasn’t passing his BS meter.

But the good news was, my flares were intermittent. And because I had a really good poker face, he had no clue just how bad things could get. Plus, over the eighteen months since my symptoms first wreaked havoc on my life, I’d become a pro on how to mentally map out bathrooms wherever we went. I’d also order sparingly at dinner. I didn’t want to be holed up in some bathroom while he was out there wondering what he’d gotten himself into. Trying to hide my disease while also managing my day-to-day emotional spirals, however, became a lot to handle.

We finally made it to Park City, and from our balcony we could see the snow-covered mountains in the distance and the beautifully dressed celebrities in their winter wear dotting the streets below us. I couldn’t wait to wear an outfit I had been saving in my suitcase—the all-white look. We’re talking a faux fur vest and matching beanie, topped off with the cutest low-rise skinny jeans. I looked like an influencer before there even were influencers, y’all!

As Brian and I made our way to a rooftop party, I suddenly felt the urge. My eyes immediately darted to a hallway on the other side of these massive sliding glass doors. It was a single-stall bathroom and the line was too long. I had to make a move, and fast. I tugged on Brian’s sweater and whispered, “I need to run back to the hotel.” He understood it was urgent code for needing to use the bathroom. He handed me our room key, and I couldn’t have left any faster.

As I started speed-walking toward our hotel, the soft buzz of the alcohol slowly began to dissipate, and my intermittent depression began to creep in. Here we were, in this beautiful city at a dreamlike event, and it had been interrupted once again by my disease. Can’t I catch a break? I thought.

As I crossed the street to our hotel, the need to go was only intensifying. Almost there, I said to myself. Squeeze your cheeks!

I got to the elevator bank and pushed the up button several times, as if that would make the elevator move faster. I painfully watched the numbers click at a glacial pace from floor to floor: eight . . . seven . . . six . . . And then, like a volcano about to erupt, my poor body just couldn’t keep it in. I prayed it would just be some flatulence.

Luckily, no one was around, but I was devastated, embarrassed, and defeated. When I got back to the hotel room I threw away those new, gorgeous jeans that now represented something so painful. I sat and cried.

“How much longer can I live like this?” I whimpered.

I didn’t feel like going back out. I had worked too hard to prevent ulcerative colitis from stealing my joy and taking over my life. That day, I had lost the battle. I had assumed that if I could map bathrooms in every space I entered, limit what I ate, and take my medicine, situations like this wouldn’t happen. So much of ulcerative colitis was accepting that most of this was totally out of my control. I texted Brian that I was going to skip the rest of the events that afternoon. He came back and just held me on the bed.

This was the only time I ever soiled myself. But I can’t tell you the countless times I’ve busted into coffee shops and restaurants to beg for the code to the bathroom only to be told I’d need to wait in line and buy something.

They say you’re supposed to know your nearest exit. But as someone living with bowel disease, I’ve always scouted the nearest bathroom. If I was going to be traveling, I’d time my meals so that I could avoid having to make a pit stop on long car rides, train trips, or flights. I’d even get dehydrated, because I’d be so nervous that even water would trigger me. I was withering away both physically and emotionally.

It sounds dramatic, and that’s because it is. But I have managed to find the humor. I can even laugh (a little) now at what happened at Sundance and say to myself, Well, at least Brad Pitt wasn’t standing in the elevator next to me.

The plot was foiled after the would-be accomplices failed to gain entry to the victims’ home, while Barr’s phone later exposed his role.

A Scottish court sentenced Robert Barr to eight years' imprisonment for orchestrating an attempted £2 million ($2.7 million) cryptocurrency theft from his prison cell at HMP Edinburgh.

Barr was serving a 21-month sentence for cryptocurrency-related fraud when he organized the operation. The High Court in Glasgow sentenced him alongside Sean Favier, who received four years, and Iain Doyle, who was jailed for five years.

The trio pleaded guilty to involvement in serious organized crime prior to their sentencing, the court said in a statement on Tuesday.

According to the court's account, the plan relied on AnyDesk, software that allows users to access and control another computer remotely. Barr wanted his accomplices to get inside the victims' home and make the homeowner download the program, allowing him to control the couple's computer remotely from prison.

Once connected, Barr planned to enter a receiving cryptocurrency address and move funds from the victims' wallet into accounts under his control.

However, the plan didn't get that far. The court heard that Favier and Doyle arrived at a couple's home at about 11:30 p.m. on April 17, 2024, but the occupants spotted them on their doorbell camera and refused to open the door. The pair left without gaining entry.

"This was a crime which married 21st-century computer sophistication with old-fashioned housebreaking," Lord Cubie said when sentencing the men.

The court was told that investigators uncovered Barr's failed heist after seizing his phone on June 25, 2024 and finding messages detailing his role in and instructions to Favier and Doyle.

Addressing Barr's previous conviction on crypto-related fraud, the judge said his decision to organize another offence from prison was a "material aggravating factor."

"In terms of the sentence to be imposed if you had been found guilty after trial, I would have imposed a sentence of eight years and ten months," the judge said.

Barr faces a serious crime prevention hearing on Nov. 17.

#5058. Elon Musk Calls Claude Opus 5.5 a 'Masterpiece', Admits Grok 4.8 Won't Match It

Elon Musk Calls Claude Opus 5.5 a 'Masterpiece', Admits Grok 4.8 Won't Match It

Elon Musk has given a rival AI model an unusually enthusiastic endorsement while acknowledging that his own next release won't be able to beat it. Asked how Grok 4.8 would compare with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, the xAI founder answered it would be “not as good.”

“Opus 5.5 is a masterpiece,” Musk posted on X.

The admission came in a reply on X Tuesday to a question from a user named Dimdv. Musk added that Grok 5, a next generation model that will be released after this update, “should exceed Opus 5.5,” potentially in two or three months, although he gave further details for that prediction or a firm date for its release—and he’s known for not sticking to his own target dates.

For a company trying to catch up with Anthropic and OpenAI, the distinction matters. Grok 4.8 is the update Musk expects to put in some users' hands this week; Grok 5 is the model he believes could eventually put his company ahead, until competing AI companies release a new model.

The exchange began with a technical update in which Musk said Grok 4.8 had finished pretraining but was still undergoing reinforcement learning, or RL, a phase in which a model's responses are refined using feedback and rewards. He said the team had also spent considerable time cleaning up supervised fine-tuning data, the examples used to teach the model how to follow instructions.

Musk said the company had abandoned JAX, a machine-learning framework, and SGLang, software used to serve AI models, in favor of an inference and reinforcement-learning system rewritten in C and C++. Inference is the process of generating answers after a user sends a prompt; rewriting the underlying software can offer engineers more control over performance, though Musk provided no figures showing the resulting gains.

Developer tetsuo celebrated the announcement with “C wins again,” prompting Musk to clarify that the code was “C with a little C++.” He subsequently credited Starlink engineers with work that helped produce the Grok training and inference stack, pointing to SpaceX's practice of writing its own headers and handling precise time calculations, including leap seconds.

Musk described Grok 4.8 as “not yet incredible” but said its foundations were finally built correctly. He expects a soft rollout to Bot users later this week, giving the company an early test before any broader release.

Anthropic released Opus 5.5 on September 22, delivering a performance comparable to its higher-end Fable 5.1 model on most work while costing 40% less to run than the previous Opus version on typical workloads. The model targets difficult programming jobs and tasks in which AI agents work through multiple steps with limited human assistance.

On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which tests whether AI agents can complete complicated tasks in a command-line environment and scores them by the percentage successfully finished, Anthropic reported 66.4% for Opus 5.5 versus 57.9% for OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. Grok is very far behind in the leaderboards.

Musk has not published Grok 4.8 scores that would establish how large the gap really is. His immediate target is the limited rollout later this week; the promised Grok 5 challenge to Opus 5.5 is still, by his own estimate, two or three months away.

#5056. Bitcoin Core discloses three patched security flaws, including high-severity mining bug

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Thousands of Bitcoin nodes granted trusted permissions to incoming Tor connections under certain configurations, according to one of the advisories.

Bitcoin Core publicly disclosed three security vulnerabilities on Tuesday, including a high-severity flaw that could prevent affected mining nodes from creating valid block templates.

The earliest of the three was reported in April 2025, with the other two reported in September last year. Bitcoin Core, the software used by many Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) nodes, issued fixes for each of them in October 2025.

The high-severity CVE-2025-62861 affected Bitcoin Core versions 28.0 to 28.2 and 29.0 to 29.1. Niklas Goegge reported it on Sept. 26, 2025. Bitcoin Core's TRUC "sibling eviction" rules were still being applied to transactions returning to the mempool after a chain reorganization. The bug could evict a transaction without removing its descendants, leaving the mempool inconsistent. Miners affected by the issue had to restart their nodes before they could create valid block templates again.

Eugene Siegel reported the medium-severity CVE-2025-62859 issue in April 2025. The vulnerability meant a malicious peer could exploit witness malleation in compact blocks to delay block processing by up to 10 minutes. The advisory said the attack could be repeated indefinitely against nodes running in "-blocksonly" mode, or where the attacker controlled all three high-bandwidth peers.

Bitcoin Core 30.0 shipped with fixes for all three vulnerabilities on Oct. 10, 2025, followed by version 29.2 on Oct. 14, 2025. The last vulnerable Bitcoin Core version went end of life on Oct. 27 this year, according to the advisories.

In May, The Block reported on a separate high-severity memory safety vulnerability that developers had also patched before publicly disclosing it.

Layer-1 blockchain network Initia confirmed Wednesday that it has suffered its second security exploit in less than three weeks, with an attacker stealing about $3.27 million in crypto assets after compromising the platform’s cloud infrastructure.

On Wednesday, Initia said the attacker gained unauthorized access on Monday through a command injection attack involving a compromised Google Cloud Platform key. The company said the breach exposed environment variables, allowing the attacker to access Initia’s GitHub and cloud accounts and obtain additional credentials.

According to Initia, the attacker accessed Anvil, a platform hosting rollups, and validated fraudulent Inter-Blockchain Communication (IBC) withdrawals from five rollups, releasing assets held in the network’s escrow accounts.

Initia said about $2.16 million of the stolen assets remain frozen on its halted network. The attacker sold assets on Initia’s decentralized exchange and withdrew 13,400 TIA, 8,000 USDC.inj and 597,000 Noble USDC. No INIT tokens were withdrawn.

Initia halted its layer-1 on Tuesday and said it intends to restore the backing of affected assets. The blockchain said recovery efforts are ongoing with its law enforcement and security partners.

The incident follows an Oct. 23 exploit that saw an attacker drain about $2.7 million after exploiting a vulnerability in Initia’s MoveVM script cache. This allowed malicious code to bypass security checks and create unbacked token balances that were subsequently bridged out of the network.

#5053. Meet the Athlete-Turned-Founder Rethinking the Sports Bra

Sara Falkson turned her own experience with ill-fitting sports bras into a brand focused on better support.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

When an athlete suits up for competition, every piece of equipment matters. A shin guard that doesn’t fit or football pads that aren’t secured properly can affect performance. But one essential piece of gear is often overlooked: the sports bra.

When shopping at top athletic retailers, female athletes are usually presented with around three options: small, medium, and large. The cup size grows with the band size, and there is little to no room for customization.

Anyone with breasts can relate to struggling to find a comfortable bra, but it's an unfortunate reality many female athletes have come to accept. What may seem like a trivial aspect of an athlete’s uniform holds a much greater significance. According to a 2021 survey of 70 elite athletes conducted by the English Institute of Sport, 75 percent of athletes have never been fitted for a sports bra, and 26 percent reported that breast pain affects their athletic performance. This speaks to the bigger picture that 46 percent of school-aged women said their breasts were a barrier to exercise.

Trying to find the solution for an ill-fitting sports bra often falls on the consumer—but Robyn founder Sara Falkson wants to change that.

Falkson grew up in a bustling home filled with love for sports and love for one another. In the middle with three older brothers and one younger sister, she tried almost every sport, but eventually settled on field hockey.

Playing sports while going through puberty is something all adolescents have to deal with, and Falkson was no exception. Navigating a changing body and mind can be tricky, especially when you’re relying on that body to remember plays and execute drills.

When it came time for the obligatory mall trip to shop for sports bras, Falkson says she found herself relying on her teammates.

“My teammates were really the best sisters of all,” she tells Women’s Health. “I found such a family and community in sports.”

Her teammates offered emotional support, but Falkson still struggled to find physical support.

“I have a bigger chest, and when it came to finding a sports bra, I struggled so deeply,” she says. “I would either find some that would be over-sexualizing, or I would chafe, and I would get horrible scars and stabs.”

A solution she and her mom came up with was for her to wear two sports bras while playing field hockey. Although this remedy did solve the support issue, Falkson says it came with another set of issues—teammates commented on it, and it wasn’t comfortable.

“Early on, I just assumed that my body’s probably the problem,” she says. “This gear design came from huge companies. They know what they’re doing, and I’m probably the one not fitting the mold.”

This prompted her to look toward other solutions, such as modifying her fueling regime to change her body, as well as the more permanent solution of a breast reduction.

These experiences stayed with Falkson, including through her time on the Dartmouth College field hockey team. She says that even in college, a lot of her teammates were still navigating the same issues of pressure and appearance on the field.

“We tried to do as much as possible to bring in the resources on the mental performance side and the nutrition side at Dartmouth and really switch the language [to] being more performance-focused, rather than appearance,” she says.

After earning her undergraduate degree, Falkson moved to San Francisco and began coaching youth field hockey on the side. She loved coaching, but soon heard familiar concerns from her players.

“The girls were saying the exact same things,” she says. “They were focused more on how they looked in their uniforms than how they were actually performing, and by that point, I’m like, ‘This is ridiculous. Why do so many of us feel this way?’”

Motivated by her frustration, Falkson enrolled at Harvard University to pursue a master’s degree in design and engineering. While there, a single stat stayed on her mind: 50 percent of girls drop out of sport by age 14 due to low body confidence, according to research conducted by Dove.

“It was so heartbreaking, but also in some ways validating knowing that there’s some research grounded in this, and we’re not alone,” she says.

While at Harvard, Falkson started leading body confidence workshops in the Boston area where she sat down with young female athletes to get a better understanding on what could be done to help them feel better about playing sports.

“We put the ownership in their hands, and that’s how we got Robyn,” she says of her company, an athletic brand dedicated to designing sports bras that elevate body confidence on and off the field. “Time after time, girls were so frustrated about sports bras, because they’re an essential piece of equipment, but so overlooked.”

Robyn started as a master’s thesis proposal. Falkson’s advisor, Karen Korellis Reuther, played a key role.

Korellis Reuther is extremely familiar with the world of design. Now a Design Critic in Architecture in Harvard’s Graduate School of Design, she is a designer by training and practice for over 40 years and is a former creative executive at Nike and Reebok.

Korellis Reuther’s passion for helping to redesign the world for women also was fueled by personal experience.

“As designers, we really connect very much to the built world, and that’s where Sara really had a passion,” Korellis Reuther says, “We were trying to understand what around the built world—whether it’s what we put on our bodies, what we use, or what we surround ourselves with—that is causing girls’ body confidence to drop, and what could we do from a design perspective?”

Korellis Reuther’s research in women-focused design goes far beyond sports. She is the author of Man-Made: How We Designed a World That Leaves Women Out, and How We Can Make It Right.

In the book, Korellis Reuther explores how women are still grossly unaccounted for in the world of design, despite inhabiting the same world as men. Her research examines how components of everyday life inconvenience women—and sometimes endanger them.

From poor locker room setups to unfit fire equipment gear for female firefighters and personal protection equipment, women are consistently thought of as an afterthought when it comes to design.

“We think, ‘I can’t make this work,’” she says. “But the truth is, it wasn’t designed for us in the first place.”

While working as a design executive for major brands, Korellis Reuther had a unique perspective being physically present where these decisions were made, but still not feeling like change was taking place. She speaks openly about feeling dismissed and looked over in important meetings, despite her high-ranking position in the company.

“The story had to be told, and as a designer, I knew we could make it right.”

Robyn is set to release a high-support bra, the Game Day, and a medium-support bra, the Everyday. The principal component that makes Robyn bras different from other athletic brands is the adjustability features. Almost all components of the bra will be adjustable, including the shoulder straps and bottom band.

In preliminary testing, subjects ran at 8 MPH pace while hooked up to machines to monitor their breast movement. The Robyn Bra demonstrated approximately 46 percent less vertical breast movement than a leading high-support sports bra.

Robyn encompasses Falkson, including the brand’s name. She and her mother share Robyn as a middle name. It proved to have a double meaning after Korellis Reuther pointed out that the robin is one of the only species of bird with a distinct breast that is a different color then the rest of the body.

“Just like the robin bird, we want our athlete to lead with color, joy, and strength,” Falkson says.

Robyn has certainly been led with strength thus far. With the product set to launch this spring, Robyn has already amassed over 34,000 followers on Instagram as well as more than 100 brand ambassadors comprised of high school and college athletes.

It has already been a part of five major collaborations, and was featured in Yankees Mag—another element that’s personal to Falkson, as her longtime boyfriend, Ben Rice, plays professional baseball for the New York Yankees.

The couple went to high school together and began dating early in college. Rice will make the occasional surprise appearance on Robyn’s social media, like when Falkson handmade a coffee table to celebrate his anniversary with the team. She also filmed a series in which she 3D printed custom Yankees memorabilia for this year’s playoff season.

Both athletes, Falkson says the two are able to push each other to be better, and seeing Rice’s career expand has made her more inspired about her own.

“I think if anything, seeing his career has just inspired me to also push to see my dreams and take risks,” she says.

Robyn isn’t just about apparel—it has its own mission, too. The company has hosted dozens of body confidence workshops, including a recent partnership with South Bronx United, a soccer nonprofit.. Robyn teamed up with South Bronx United as well as mental health organization The Hidden Opponent to create a four week-curriculum focused on empowering young athletes.

Robyn also works with Shooting Touch, a basketball nonprofit out of Boston for body confidence-focused programming. Falkson also coordinated a partnership with a 3D printing company to bring the printers into local schools to encourage more girls to get into STEM.

“For me personally, I’m glad our world has Saras, because we need to keep pushing forward,” Korellis Reuther says. “She pushes forward from her true, authentic self—with a sense of joy, with a sense of optimism, but also a sense of, ‘We haven’t done it right yet, and we need to make this right.’”

Looking toward the future, Falkson says her dream scenario would be to have Robyn gear become part of a female athlete’s uniform. “Once I see Robyn in the real world and girls connecting and bonding over a body confident sport and feeling their best, celebrating lifelong movement, that’s my goal.”

Through it all, Falkson has held on to the perspective she had as a young athlete.

“Growing up and being a woman is hard,” she says. “What you’re going through is okay and normal, and you’re still going to be valued. Giving girls the resources to have that space is really important.”

Alyssa Cruz is the social media editor at Women’s Health, where she drives social strategy and helps shape the brand’s voice across platforms. Prior to WH, she worked at CBS News and palabra. Originally from Toledo, she is a proud alumna of Ohio University, where she received two bachelor’s degrees in journalism and Spanish. When she is not creating social content, you can find her trying different restaurants in New York City or planning her next trip.

#5051. OKXICE sets Nov. 23 launch for tokenized securities venue under SEC innovation exemption

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On Wednesday, OKX and ICE announced it would launch its TSV on Nov. 23 as part of the SEC's five-year innovation exemption.

OKXICE, the joint venture between OKX and NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange, plans to launch its tokenized securities venue at the end of the month, bringing the Securities and Exchange Commission's "innovation exemption" to life.

On Wednesday, OKX and ICE announced it would launch its TSV on Nov. 23 as part of the SEC's five-year innovation exemption that debuted in September to bring capital markets in the U.S. on-chain and not have to register as more traditional exchanges.

"The future of finance is onchain, and we have an opportunity to build it here in America, with the standards, safeguards and ambition that investors expect,” said former New York Governor and Co-Chair of OKXICE Andrew Cuomo, in a statement.

The announcement of the launch comes amid dozens of issuers that say they have objected to tokenized versions of their stock trading on OKXICE. As part of the innovation exemption, issuers can decide that they don't want their stock to trade on certain venues. In the latest filing from Nov. 5, 67 companies had opted out, including Meta Platforms, Inc. The Home Depot, Netflix, Tesla, and Costco.

On Wednesday, ICE and OKX said it has confirmed 70 assets so far from issuers including Coinbase, Circle and Robinhood, as well as 59 exchange-traded funds. The OKXICE's TSV is available to customers in the U.S. who have a CeDeFi Wallet and have completed onboarding, the companies said.

A few reasons have since been reported for why companies objected to trading on OKXICE. A spokesperson for one of the companies that opted out, Applied Optoelectronics, told the Wall Street Journal the fiber-optic maker objected because it was unsure how tokenization would affect its stock price, liquidity and volatility, and also had concerns about whether investors may be confused about the company's involvement in the offering.

Another major exchange, Nasdaq is also working on tokenization and has partnered with crypto exchange Kraken on it. In late September, the exchange posted a Q&A on the SEC's innovation exemption. Nasdaq has taken a different view in that it has pushed back against the SEC's innovation exemption and has said it plans to "opt its own stock out of Tokenized Securities Venues," said Nasdaq Chief Legal and Regulatory Officer John Zecca in an op-ed published by Barron's on Tuesday.

Zecca said tokenization can be a positive for share issuers, but said a framework for tokenization should protect the rights attached to the underlying shares, uphold the principle that a tokenized stock remains a stock, and ensure issuers have a meaningful role in shaping how their shares are tokenized.

"Our greater concern, however, is that the Innovation Exemption allows tokenized securities to trade outside the government-regulated National Market System, which maintains a market data, reporting, and transparency framework that all stock trading must abide by," Zecca said, adding that fragmentation could then occur.

#5050. SEC enforcement actions fall 24%, crypto cases in spotlight

The SEC filed 348 actions in fiscal 2026, down from 456 a year earlier. Cases included alleged Bitcoin mining fraud and an FTX audit settlement.

The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filed 348 enforcement actions in fiscal 2026, down 23.7% from 456 a year earlier.

Its annual enforcement results included cases involving alleged crypto fraud and failures in FTX’s audits.

In its Tuesday release, the SEC said it had charged three purported crypto trading platforms and four investment clubs in an alleged scheme that defrauded investors of at least $14 million. In a separate case, the agency accused the founder of a Bitcoin mining business of misappropriating $48.5 million after raising more than $95.6 million from about 6,400 investors.

In April, the SEC settled charges against Francis Decker, the Prager Metis partner who led FTX’s audits, over failures to meet professional auditing standards.

In February, a jury found Ismael Zarco Sanchez liable for securities fraud and registration violations over his role in the $300 million CryptoFX Ponzi scheme. In July, a court ordered Michael Noble to pay $1.07 million in a case over his role promoting BitConnect’s crypto lending program.

Fiscal 2026 was SEC Chair Paul Atkins’ first full fiscal year in office. The 348 enforcement actions were the agency’s fewest since 1991, according to a Reuters review of SEC records. Standalone actions fell to 235 from 303 a year earlier.

The decline in crypto enforcement was already visible in 2025, when the SEC filed 13 crypto-related actions, down from 33 in 2024, according to Cornerstone Research. Five of the 13 were filed before former Chair Gary Gensler left office in January 2025.

The SEC said its new enforcement analytics office was using “blockchain and financial-flow analysis” to detect potential misconduct earlier.

#5049. Near AI Breach Exposes User Details and Data From 18 AI Agents

Near AI Breach Exposes User Details and Data From 18 AI Agents

Near AI has disclosed a breach that exposed account information belonging to about 100 users and data from 18 AI agents after an attacker exploited software running its servers.

The company said in a November 9 report that an attacker used a remote code execution vulnerability in SGLang, an open-source engine that runs AI models and generates responses to user requests.

The exploit allowed the intruder to execute commands on one inference server and then reach other parts of Near AI’s infrastructure.

Investigators traced the intrusion to an internal system connected to Private Chat, a feature the company had already retired. The attacker downloaded names and email addresses for approximately 100 users, along with subscription plan and account balance information for some of them.

Another 18 agents were accessed on an older deployment of Near AI Agents, where the attacker retrieved their chat histories, settings and logs. Those agents were not running inside NEAR AI’s confidential computing environment, which is designed to shield information from the company operating the servers.

Logs also exposed NEAR AI Cloud API keys belonging to two customers. These keys function like digital credentials that applications use to access cloud services; Near AI says it has revoked both, but did not say whether the attacker used them.

Near AI found no indication that stored Private Chat conversations or uploaded files had been accessed. The confirmed theft involved account records and legacy agent data, while exposure of live confidential requests remains a possibility identified by the investigation.

Hardware isolation does not guarantee that the software inside the protected environment is safe. “It does not protect against a vulnerability in the software running inside the environment,” Near AI acknowledged, explaining that the SGLang flaw let the attacker run code where confidential requests were being processed.

SGLang had already attracted scrutiny from security researchers. In July, Carnegie Mellon University’s CERT Coordination Center documented six vulnerabilities in the project, including bugs that could let attackers execute commands or expose credentials, depending on how servers were configured.

Near AI did not identify the specific SGLang flaw exploited in this incident, so there is no basis to link the breach to any of those earlier disclosures. It reported the vulnerability to SGLang’s developers.

Near, to its credit, was quick to fix the issues.

“On detection, we revoked all active sessions and administrative credentials, replaced all agent tokens, took Private Chat offline, and deployed a fix for the SGLang vulnerability across all inference servers,” the project said.

”We've completed the rotation of all remaining credentials and a full forensic review. We have notified users whose account details or agents we have confirmed were accessed and will make any regulatory notifications that are required.”

Near AI notified users whose account records or agents it confirmed were accessed and says it will make any required regulatory notifications. It also warned users to be wary of unsolicited messages referring to their Near AI accounts or balances, and contacted the owners of all 18 affected agents individually.

#5044. Nvidia Erases 2026 Gains as Republicans Threaten Jensen Huang With Subpoena

Nvidia Erases 2026 Gains as Republicans Threaten Jensen Huang With Subpoena

Nvidia shares plunged to $166.95 Tuesday afternoon, leaving the AI chipmaker down 18.42% for November and wiping out all the gains it had accumulated in 2026.

The selloff accelerated as congressional Republicans threatened to subpoena CEO Jensen Huang over his reported relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.

At that price, Nvidia was roughly 10.5% below its $186.50 closing price at the end of 2025 and 31.4% below its recent $243.37 peak. November is shaping up as its worst month since September 2022, when shares lost roughly 19.6%; the company suffered an even deeper 32% crash in April of that year.

Tuesday's drop exceeded 6% in afternoon trading, after a 4.3% fall on Monday. The two-day decline was on track to erase more than $470 billion in market value. Even after the significant drop, some analysts would still view the stock as extremely overbought in the long term, with prices much higher than what would be considered safe based on technical indicators.

Just for context, even an additional 20% crash (-43% from October) would be considered healthy in an isolated technical analysis, leaving the price still above the average price of the last 50 months. Prices tend to either bounce or trade near that line. When prices go too far away from the average, that usually means there is an unusual appetite for the asset, typically driven more by FOMO than fundamentals.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast told ABC News on Tuesday that he was prepared to subpoena Huang unless the CEO responded by Wednesday, November 11, to a request for a closed-door briefing. No subpoena had been issued at the time of the report.

Mast and two other Republican committee chairs asked Huang to appear on November 18 and explain his interactions with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed. The lawmakers also want details about Nvidia's safeguards against foreign espionage, according to a letter reviewed by Reuters.

U.S. authorities have reportedly investigated whether Alice Huang, who has no family relationship to the Nvidia CEO, passed information to Beijing. The allegations have not established that Jensen Huang knowingly disclosed confidential information or violated export rules.

On Sunday, Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation into whether its chief executive was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The board said it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets were compromised, but would examine the available information.

Earlier today, the Financial Times reported Nvidia has hired former U.S. prosecutor Joon H Kim to conduct the internal investigation.

The company is also facing legal pressure. Shareholders filed a proposed class-action lawsuit Monday alleging that Nvidia and Huang failed to disclose risks associated with the reported relationship.

The scandal has landed during a broader reassessment of the AI boom. Investors have questioned how long massive spending on data centers can continue, and Nvidia's competitors are offering customers more alternatives to its expensive chips.

Google introduced new AI chip configurations Monday. The Information reported that OpenAI was considering buying Google's tensor processing units, or TPUs, which are processors built specifically to run AI workloads. Neither company has confirmed a purchase but yesterday Google announced a new line of TPUs available for select customers, directly competing against Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly earnings on November 17, one day before the congressional briefing requested by House Republicans. Mast's deadline for Huang to respond comes first, on November 11.

#5042. Bitcoin ‘ripe for a squeeze’ as options traders raise odds of sub-$70,000 Christmas

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Derive's Christmas bitcoin options pricing has turned increasingly bearish over the past week, while K33 said the cryptocurrency is set for a squeeze in either direction.

Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) was trading around $73,500 on Wednesday after recording five consecutive weekly losses, with options traders now pricing a greater chance of the largest cryptocurrency dropping below $70,000 by Christmas than climbing above $80,000.

Last Wednesday, the platform put the odds of an $80,000-plus finish at 53%. That has now fallen to 26%, according to Derive founder and CEO Nick Forster, while the chance of a sub-$70,000 Christmas finish has risen from 15% to 31%.

Forster told The Block that traders are becoming increasingly defensive, with downside protection (puts) costing more than equivalent upside exposure (calls). Bitcoin options trading on Derive totaled $418 million last week, a 37% increase, and puts accounted for 55% of premiums traded compared to the previous week's share of 36%, he said.

"One of the most interesting trades came just hours before Thursday's tech sell-off, when a wallet spent approximately $14K protecting 300 BTC against a fall below $60K by November 27," Forster said. "The position could pay up to $3 million if bitcoin falls below $50K."

Bitcoin dropped back below $74,000 on Tuesday following the release of October's U.S. consumer price index. Prices increased 0.4% during the month against expectations of 0.3%, and futures traders priced in further Fed tightening at the December meeting. That followed more than $1 billion in crypto long liquidations on Monday as bitcoin fell below its 50-week moving average, with Friday's U.S. producer price index release next on the economic calendar.

Meanwhile, perpetual futures open interest stood at around 353,000 BTC on Tuesday, according to K33's latest research report, only higher on 1.2% of trading days over the previous two years.

Over the past 30 days, open interest increased 12%, and bitcoin lost 10%, K33 Head of Research Vetle Lunde noted, with open interest climbing to levels last seen near the October 2025 peak, towards the end of the November 2025 selloff, and ahead of the August rally.

"A breakdown could trigger substantial long liquidations, while a recovery could fuel short covering, amplifying price moves as leveraged positions unwind," Lunde said, adding that the market was "ripe for a squeeze."

K33 also noted a 0.75 correlation between bitcoin and the Nasdaq over 30 days, a reading in the 99th percentile since 2020. Reviewing 16 previous strong Nasdaq rebounds from market corrections, of the nine that continued higher, bitcoin gained in eight, Lunde said, with a median return of 2.9% over 20 days. Bitcoin fell in each of the seven failed rebounds, with a median loss of 21% in the following 20 days.

Meanwhile, U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs recorded net outflows of $1.28 billion last week, with a further $296 million exiting the ETFs on Monday and Tuesday, according to data compiled by The Block, as the funds also turned negative for the year. Global bitcoin ETPs have recorded withdrawals of 31,652 BTC over the past seven trading days, according to K33.
